releases.title: Teardrops as copper regions; Live Simulation's own button and symbols; a tidier desktop

items.text: Tools › Teardrops now makes each teardrop a region of copper on the track's layer, as the desktop software does, in place of the short arcs or tracks it used to add. Its window sets the working mode (Add or Remove), the objects (All or Selected only), the style (Curved or Line), Force teardrops, Adjust teardrop size and Generate report, and four kinds of joint, each with its tick, its sizes in per cent and a drawing that follows the sizes as you type them: Via/TH Pad, SMD Pad, Tracks (where a track changes width) and T-Junction. A teardrop is made smaller where the full one would come too close to other copper, a joint that has one gets no second, and Remove takes them off again, those of earlier versions too. In the board's file each is marked as a teardrop the way the desktop software marks its own, and the teardrops of its boards are known as such here.
items.alt: A routed example board near a microcontroller, its tracks widening into curved teardrops where they meet vias and pads, with the Teardrops window in front: Working Mode, Objects, the Options, and under Scope the four kinds of joint, each with a drawing of its teardrop and its sizes in per cent.

items.text: Live Simulation has a button of its own at the right of the menu bar, quiet until a sheet runs and red while one does. With a schematic in front, that sheet runs as it is, and nothing on it is changed by running it; with anything else in front, a new circuit is opened. The panel is headed by the sheet's name, with New Circuit, Open a Circuit, Save the Circuit and Examples beside it.
items.alt: The example of a rectifier with a smoothing capacitor running in Live Simulation: the wires coloured by their voltage, two test points with their readings, the Live Simulation panel headed by the sheet's name with its four icons, and the Live Scope drawing the supply's sine wave and the smoothed output.

items.text: Live Simulation's parts can be drawn the European or the American way: the resistor, the potentiometer, the capacitor, the polarised capacitor and the inductor have a drawing for each. Choose under Symbols in the panel, and the parts already on the sheet are redrawn where they stand, still on their wires. A Polarised capacitor is in the palette (Polarized capacitor with the American symbols); while a sheet runs, one with its voltage the wrong way round is ringed and listed.

The panels start in a new arrangement: Projects, the Storage Manager and the Inspector docked on the left, and Libraries, Requirements, Calculators and the Clipboard behind tabs on the right edge, where pointing at a tab slides its panel out. The first start of this version brings your desktop to it once, for those panels only: what else you have open stays where it is. Every other panel opens from View › Workspace Panels or the panel buttons of the status bar.
Tools › Update From Libraries no longer takes a simulation model's own values away from it.

In a browser without a folder picker (Firefox, Safari), the button that asks for a project's folder did nothing. It now asks through the browser's own folder window, and the project opens with its documents.
Interactive routing no longer pushes other tracks when every pushing mode is unticked in Preferences › PCB Editor › Interactive Routing: the mode in force is always one of those ticked.

In the 3D view the board stays sharp when you zoom in: once the view rests, the part in view is painted again finely. A layer shown alone there (Shift+S) is copper like the rest of the view, whichever layer it is.
konium.app now says at the top of its first page that Konium Designer is free, and exactly what free does not cover.

releases.title: The source code is public

items.text: Konium Designer's source code is now public, under the GNU General Public License (version 3 or later): anyone may read it, build it, change it and pass it on under the same licence. Help › About has the way to it (Source Code), the licence in full (Licence..., kept in your copy so it shows without a connection) and the software of others that is built in, each with its own licence (Third-Party Software...). Ask to Audit the Source Code is gone from About: nobody has to ask any more. In its place, Help › Contact the Author takes a security problem reported privately.
items.alt: Help › About over the demo board with Third-Party Software open: a list of the packages built into Konium Designer, each with its version and its licence, and a field to search them.

items.text: Before the source went out, the whole program and the services behind konium.app were gone through for what a stranger could do with a crafted file, a script or a request, and for what could lose or damage a design. What was found is fixed, each with a test that shows it, and the record is in the repository. A script run from Tools › Scripts, and a document made to mislead, can do no more than they are meant to; the pages Konium Designer writes (reports, prints) can run nothing.

A footprint's own vias (thermal vias under a part) now belong to their part: they move, turn and go with it, where before they stayed behind when the part was moved. Deleting or exploding a polygon pour on a board with internal planes no longer disturbs the planes' edges.

Safer saving and recovery. After a crash, the copies kept for recovery are no longer lost when a document of the same name is closed or saved in another window, and a recovered copy opens beside an open document of its name. A Save As that is cancelled no longer changes the format the next Save writes. A save to a place the browser cannot write no longer leaves an empty file that passes for the saved one: the document is downloaded instead, and a window says so. If the browser refuses to keep an auto-saved copy because its storage is full, that is said.

Said, where before nothing was: a second file with the name of a document that is already open is not opened, and Konium Designer now says so instead of showing the first as if it were the second; a STEP export names the parts whose 3D models it could not write; a script of your own is asked about before it is deleted.

With network activity off, the browser is now told to refuse every kind of thing a page can load, scripts, style sheets and workers among them, and nothing at all is asked of konium.app. The one thing no web page can stop is stated in the list of connections: for a copy at konium.app, or installed from it, the browser itself looks for newer offline files about once a day (a downloaded copy has none of that). What the Component Builder reads from a datasheet is shared for the next person only when the datasheet came from the web, never when you opened it from your computer.
Single layer mode in the 3D view: Shift+S shows the layer in front alone there too, without the parts' bodies, and follows the layer as you change it.
items.alt: The demo board in the 3D view in single layer mode: the top layer's copper alone on the bare board, with a note saying Single layer mode: Top Layer alone.

items.text: One style for Konium Designer's own panels (the power, thermal, EMC, supply impedance and antenna analyses, the Layout Planner, the Smart Router and the rest): a section's name small above it, its tools as icons with their names, and the one action that runs it filled. On the dark theme the colour icons of the toolbars and menus are now light, and the download button in Get Konium Designer can be read.
items.alt: The EMC Check panel beside the demo board: What to check and Rules as small headings over aligned fields, a filled Check button, and under Results one finding about supply pins with no capacitor close by.

items.text: Bug reports take large attachments: over 8 MB together they are zipped and sent in parts, 40 MB zipped at most.

releases.title: The Layout Planner, the Smart Router and free-flowing routes

items.text: Layout Planner (Tools › Layout Planner, in the PCB editor): the AI model you chose plans where a board's parts go before any of them is placed. The plan gives the groups of parts that belong together and where each group sits, the parts that must be at an edge, what must be close to which pin (a decoupling capacitor at its supply pin, a crystal at the oscillator pins), and what must be kept apart or clear, each with its reason, and draws the groups as zones over the board. Place by the Plan then puts every part in its exact place in one step, and each thing the plan asked is marked as met or not as the board stands. Plan Again sends the plan back with what was not met and what you want changed. The model is never asked for coordinates: it decides, and the placer measures.
items.alt: The Layout Planner panel beside its example board after Place by the Plan: the parts placed inside the outline, and in the panel the plan's summary, the result of the placing and the groups.

items.text: Smart Router (Tools › Smart Router): the model plans how the placed board is routed, as a layout engineer decides it before routing: which nets are routed alike, how wide, on which layers, with how many vias and in what order, the via size, what is poured, and which nets are differential pairs, each with its reason. Make the Rules writes that as the board's own net classes and design rules. Route by the Plan has the autorouter carry it out in one step: the pads of poured nets are joined to their pour by a via, a track wider than its pad is necked down there, and a differential pair's two tracks are laid side by side at its gap where that can be done. The result lists what was routed and what was left, class by class, and what the design rule check finds that was not there before. Plan Again sends that back to the model.
items.alt: The Smart Router panel beside the example board routed by a plan: tracks on the top layer over a ground pour on the bottom, and in the panel the result of the run and the classes in the order they were routed.

items.text: Plan, Place and Route (Tools › Plan, Place and Route): the planner and the router as one run, from a board with its parts beside the outline to a routed board, ending with the design rule check. It stops after each stage for your go-ahead, so that a plan can be read, and changed in its own panel, before it is carried out; untick that and it runs through.

Free-flowing routes: a routing style in which a track takes the direct way at any angle and curves in an arc round each pad, via or track it passes, as a rubber band would lie. Choose it in Preferences › PCB Editor › Interactive Routing › Routing Style for the autorouter, the Smart Router and the routes you place by hand, or reshape routes that are already there with Route › Make Free-Flowing. The tracks come out shorter and run beside each other for less of their length, which lowers crosstalk; there is no corner to disturb a microwave line, or for a crack to start at on a flexible board. For ordinary digital signals 45° corners do no harm, and there the choice is one of taste.
items.alt: The example board routed free-flowing: tracks at many angles that curve in arcs round pads and vias, several in concentric curves beside the microcontroller.

items.text: These tools work like the other AI tools: off until you switch AI on, started by hand, and each says what it will send and to whom before anything goes. A board's outline, parts and nets go as text; no drawing does. How good a plan is depends on the model you choose, so read a plan before you carry it out. Each step is one Undo.
Route › Fanout no longer puts the vias of two neighbouring pads on top of each other: a fanout's via keeps the Hole To Hole Clearance rule's distance from every other hole.

The User Guide opens where you left it. Leave its tab for a document and come back, and it is at the same chapter, as far down the page, with the same search, where it used to start again at its beginning. The guide has new sections for the Layout Planner, the Smart Router, free-flowing routes and Plan, Place and Route.

releases.title: Where each connection goes, and EDIF text in its own sizes

items.text: The list of what Konium Designer connects to now says where each connection actually goes. Its To column names every party what you send reaches, in order: the address your browser asks, then whoever that passes it on to. AI jobs through the Konium service go to konium.app, then OpenRouter, then the company that runs the model you chose; with your own key they go straight from your browser to OpenRouter or the provider you gave, and with a local model nowhere but your own computer or network. Digi-Key and Mouser searches go to konium.app and from there to Digi-Key or Mouser. JLCPCB lookups go to jlcsearch.tscircuit.com, a public copy of JLCPCB's parts list, not to JLCPCB itself. A bug report goes to konium.app, then the author's mailbox and the author's private repository at GitHub, where the author and the AI assistant that helps build Konium Designer read it. Nothing that is sent has changed, only what the list says of it.
items.alt: Preferences, System, Network Activity: the Connections table from its AI rows down. AI jobs through the Konium service go to konium.app, then OpenRouter, then the company OpenRouter has run the chosen model; with your own key straight from your browser to OpenRouter or the address you gave; a local model at the address you gave. Then datasheets for the AI tools, shared AI results, JLCPCB lookups at jlcsearch.tscircuit.com (a public copy, not JLCPCB itself), Digi-Key and Mouser through konium.app, and bug reports to konium.app and the author's mailbox.

items.text: Links have a row of their own in that list: a page your browser opens when you click, such as Ko-fi for a donation, a part's page at a supplier or a datasheet's address. Konium Designer sends nothing there, and switching network activity off does not stop a click of yours. The list is the same in Help › About, Preferences › System › Network Activity, the User Guide and the website's FAQ.

EDIF schematics: texts in their own sizes. A file from xDX Designer says how high each text is, and designators, values, net names, notes and pin names now take a font of that size, where every text was 10 points. The lines of a note stand as far apart as their size asks.

The User Guide has four more pictures: a netlist loaded into a board as an Engineering Change Order, the Selection Filter, a part over its rating in Live Simulation with Solve for a value set up, and a footprint from the IPC wizard in 3D.

releases.title: EDIF schematics from xDX Designer, and the list of overlapping objects

items.text: EDIF schematics from xDX Designer (.eds) open, and as they were drawn. The file was not taken at all under that name; EDIF is now told by its content, whatever the file is called. And what that tool writes in its own way is read: the designators and pin numbers the design was given, where they read R? and C? before; each text shown or hidden as the file says, at its place on the page, where hidden part names and tolerances lay scattered across the sheet; ground and supply symbols as power ports; and a net drawn in separate pieces as one net, where a label stood on every pin.

Net names in such a file: a name shown on the sheet is a net label where it was, ending at its place where the file has it so. A name of the designer's that the file hides is kept as one label in the middle of its wire, so that the netlist is the same; a name the tool made up is left out. The import checks every pin against the net EDIF joins it to, and says so if the drawing connects anything differently.

The list of overlapping objects on a board (Display popup selection dialog) stays while the wheel turns and when Shift, Ctrl or Alt goes down. It closed on any turn of the wheel, and a free-spinning wheel or a touchpad still gliding after a zoom closed it as it came, so that a click made straight after zooming never showed it. A press elsewhere or any other key still closes it.

releases.title: Calculators, ratings and solving in Live Simulation, netlists into a board, choosing what a click takes on a board

items.text: Calculators (Tools › Calculators, in every editor): the everyday sums beside your work. A voltage divider, where any one of the input, R1, R2 and the output is found from the others and a load across R2 is taken in; parts in series and in parallel, and the partner that makes a value; an LED's resistor; RC and LC; Ohm's law and power; a regulator's feedback pair; reactance; the 555 running free and as a one-shot; and the standard values nearest a value, from E6 to E192. A divider and a feedback pair also give the nearest standard pair, with the error it makes. Type quantities as you write them: 4k7, 4R7, 100n, 2.2M.
items.alt: The Calculators panel beside the demo board: a selected track's width and length taken into the track calculator, which gives the current it carries for a 10 °C rise, its resistance and the voltage it drops

items.text: Calculators for the board, on the same formulas as Power Analysis and the Field Solver so that the figures agree: a track by IPC-2221, where any one of width, current and temperature rise is found from the other two and a length gives its resistance and the voltage it drops; a via's current, resistance, thermal resistance and inductance; the spacing for a voltage by IPC-2221B's table; and a single track's impedance, or the width for an impedance. With a board in front, From the selected track and From the selected via fill the boxes from what is selected.

Live Simulation flags a part worked beyond its rating: a resistor, potentiometer, Zener diode or transistor over its power, a capacitor over its voltage, a diode or an LED over its current is ringed on the sheet with the figure beside it and listed in the panel under Over their ratings. The rating is a parameter of the part (Power Rating, Voltage Rating, Maximum Current), shown as Rated for in the panel and changed there; a part with none takes its kind's common figure, such as a quarter of a watt for a resistor, 50 V for a capacitor and 30 mA for an LED.
items.alt: Live Simulation of an LED with a 47 Ω resistor from 5 V: the LED is ringed on the sheet with 50 mA against its 30 mA rating, and the panel lists it under Over their ratings, beside Solve for a value set to find the resistance for 20 mA

items.text: Solve for a value, in the Live Simulation panel: select a part, choose one of its values under Find its, what is to read it (a voltmeter, an ammeter or a test point on the sheet, a monitor, or the probe) and the reading you want, and Find It works the value out at the circuit's operating point, to four figures, and writes it to the part. For a resistor, a capacitor and an inductor it names the nearest standard value too.

A part of a real design on the bench: select some of a sheet and choose Design › Simulate › Run the Selection as a Sketch, or Run the Selection in the panel. The selection is copied to a schematic of its own and runs there, and the design is not touched. A supply that says its voltage in its name (+5V, 3V3, -12V) gets a DC rail of that voltage; a ground under another name (AGND, DGND, VSS) is GND there; a supply whose name says no voltage (VCC, VBAT) is named for you to place a source on.

What Live Simulation watches is kept with the sheet: the monitors you kept, the scopes side by side with what each draws, and whether a run starts with everything discharged are saved with the file and come back when it is opened. A change to them is undone like any other change to the sheet.

Seven more parts for a sketch: a four-bit shift register, a ring counter of two to ten stages, a four-input multiplexer, a four-bit DAC and a four-bit ADC, a DIAC, and a slow-blow fuse that warms with the square of its current. The palette has 77 parts and there are 55 examples, seven of them new: quick and slow-blow fuses, a dimmer with a DIAC and a TRIAC, a ring counter running a light along, a shift register, a multiplexer, a counter and a DAC making a staircase, and an ADC and a DAC back to back.

Two faults of a live run are put right. An oscillator made of transistors ran at a rate that changed with the speed setting: the two-transistor astable read 21 Hz to 28 Hz, and is 20.1 Hz at every speed now. And Repeats at for a signal that swells and fades was low: two tones beating, 440 Hz and 444 Hz, read 416 Hz and now read within one per cent.

Load a Netlist (Design › Netlist › Load a Netlist..., on a board): bring a board to a netlist file from any tool. The differences come up as an Engineering Change Order, as Update PCB shows them from the schematics: parts added from the libraries by the names of their footprints, parts and nets the file does not have taken off, and pads given their nets. One Undo takes it all back. Ten kinds of netlist are told apart by their content: the .NET netlist in brackets and its later form with named fields, Tango, PADS, Telesis, KiCad, P-CAD in both its forms, MultiWire and EDIF.
items.alt: Load a Netlist on the demo board: an Engineering Change Order for a PADS netlist, adding two components, one net and four pins to nets, all validated

items.text: A package that looks like one in 3D: a footprint from the IPC footprint wizard or the Component Builder used to get a plain box of the body's height, and now gets its package in pieces. A moulded body with its pin 1 mark, each gull-wing lead with its shoulder, slope and foot, J leads, the balls of a BGA on its substrate, the terminals of a chip part, the bands of a MELF and of a diode, the tab of a DPAK, and through-hole pins. Nothing stands above the package's height.
items.alt: An eight-pin SOIC from the IPC footprint wizard in the PCB library editor's 3D view: a dark moulded body with a pin 1 dot and eight gull-wing leads standing on their pads

items.text: Boards from the 1990s. A board saved as PCB 2.8 ASCII, the text format the board programs of that time wrote and the desktop software still saves, opens through File › Open or the Import Wizard with its components, pads, tracks, arcs, fills, vias, strings and nets. A board in the PCB 5.0 binary format opens too, where it used to open empty, and is saved in the present format. The binary boards before that (PCB 3.0 and 4.0), the binary schematics and the .ddb design databases of that time are not read: opening one now says what it is and how to bring it in.

Choosing what a click takes on a board. Where a click could take more than one thing, the list beside the cursor now offers a component's pad as the pad itself as well as the component, and tells tracks apart by their lengths. What you choose stays chosen: a press on it drags it and a double-click opens it, where the object on top used to be taken again. A pad chosen on its own opens as a pad. A click inside a component's area where none of its parts is takes the component.

Selection Filter: with nothing selected on a board, the PCB Inspector panel has a button for each kind of object (Components, 3D Bodies, Keepouts, Tracks, Arcs, Pads, Vias, Regions, Polygons, Fills, Texts, Rooms, Other) and All - On. A kind that is off is passed over by a click, left out of a selection box and not listed among overlapping objects; with Components off, a click on a component's pad takes the pad. A click that finds only kinds that are off says so.
items.alt: The PCB Inspector beside the demo board with nothing selected: the Selection Filter with a button for each kind of object, Tracks, Arcs, Pads, Vias, Regions and Polygons lit and the others off

items.text: Lock Primitives, in a component's properties, now does what it says: with it cleared, a click on one of the component's primitives takes that primitive, which moves on its own, and the component is still there to choose, second in the list and by a click inside its area. And a kind that Shift Click To Select reserves for Shift is no longer taken by a plain click when it is alone under the cursor.

Follow Mouse Trail (Preferences › PCB Editor › Interactive Routing) now works: in Walkaround Obstacles and AutoRoute On Current Layer the route follows the way the cursor went since the last click, not only where it is now. Preferred Subnet Jumper Length is used as well: Route › Add Subnet Jumpers starts from it.

Preferences › PCB Editor › Defaults lists 25 kinds of object where it listed 11: each kind of dimension, Component Body, Drill Table, Layer Stack Table, Keepout Track and Keepout Arc have defaults of their own.
A notice with a lot to say stays long enough to be read.

releases.title: Live Simulation: the sheet runs as a circuit while you draw it

items.text: Live Simulation (Design › Simulate › Live Simulation, in the schematic editor): the sheet in front runs as a circuit while you draw it. Wires and pins take the colour of their voltage, red towards the most positive, blue towards the most negative and grey at 0 V; dots move along them the way the current flows, faster for more of it; the cursor on a wire or a pin reads its voltage and its current. It runs on the same engine and part models as Mixed Sim.
items.alt: The example of a 555 timer flashing an LED, running: the wires red towards the 9 V supply and grey at 0 V with dots along them, the LED lit with a red glow, test points reading 7.43 V at the timer's output and 5.01 V on the timing capacitor; on the right the panel's palette with the parts as tiles of their symbols under Passive, Diodes and thyristors, Transistors and Amplifiers and blocks, a key in the corner of each; along the bottom the Live Scope drawing the output's square wave and the capacitor's voltage rising and falling.

items.text: Sketch with it: a palette in the panel shows 70 parts as their symbols, by kind. Passive: resistor, capacitor, polarised capacitor, inductor, potentiometer, switch, changeover switch, push button, transformer, relay, crystal and fuse. Diodes and thyristors: diode, Schottky, Zener, LED, thyristor (SCR) and TRIAC. Transistors: NPN, PNP, N and P MOSFETs, N and P JFETs and a Darlington pair. Amplifiers and blocks: an op-amp with no supply pins to wire and one with them, a comparator, an analogue switch and the four controlled sources. Logic and chips: a logic input, an inverter, AND, NAND, OR, NOR and exclusive-OR gates, a Schmitt trigger, D, JK and T flip-flops, a four-bit counter, a seven-segment decoder, a 555 timer, a voltage regulator and an optocoupler. Click one and place it; wire, ground, supply, net label and text are beside them.

Fifteen sources: DC, sine, square, triangle, sawtooth, pulse, AM, FM, swept-sine and noise voltage sources, DC and sine current sources, and three that take one wire, their other end being 0 V: a voltage rail, a signal rail and a clock. Each has its amplitude, offset, frequency and phase to set, a square wave and a clock their duty cycle, and the others what makes them: a pulse's levels and times, a modulated source's carrier, signal and depth, a sweep's two frequencies and its time, the noise's bandwidth.

Every value in the panel: select a part and the panel lists what sets it, by name and unit. A diode's forward voltage, the current it is given at, its series resistance and its breakdown voltage; a Zener's voltage; a transistor's beta; a MOSFET's threshold; a JFET's pinch-off voltage and saturation current; an op-amp's gain and how far its output swings; a potentiometer's position; a transformer's ratio; a relay's pull-in and drop-out currents; a thyristor's gate trigger and holding currents; a fuse's rating; a counter's modulus; a gate's high level. Type a value, or hold the slider under it to turn it down to a tenth or up to ten times while the circuit runs. One Undo takes back a whole turn of the slider. A part that is not from the palette lists its simulation model's parameters the same way.
items.alt: The example of the waveforms: a sine, a square, a triangle and a sawtooth source each driving a resistor, with a test point on each reading its voltage; the square source is selected and the panel lists its amplitude 1 V, offset 0 V, frequency 1k Hz, phase and duty cycle 50 %, each in a box with a slider under it; four scopes side by side along the bottom draw one waveform each.

items.text: Instruments and lights: a voltmeter, an ammeter and a test point read out beside themselves on the sheet, as the value now, its mean, its RMS or its peak to peak, and each can be drawn on a scope. They are parts of the sheet, so they are saved with it. An LED lights by its current, in the colour you give it, a lamp by its power, and a seven-segment display segment by segment: with the decoder and the counter it shows a count.
items.alt: The example of a counter on a seven-segment display, held: a 2 Hz clock into the counter, its four outputs into the decoder, the decoder's seven outputs into the display, which shows 7 in red; a logic input stands low on the counter's reset. On the right the palette at Logic and chips, with the flip-flops, the counter and the decoder among the gates, then the sources, and under Instruments and outputs the voltmeter, ammeter, test point, lamp, display and speaker; along the bottom the Live Scope drawing the clock.

items.text: Monitors anywhere: click a wire, a pin or a two-pin part and its voltage and current are read out beside it as they change. Keep it, or right-click the point and choose Monitor Here, and it stays on the sheet while you take the next; up to 24 at once.

Switches and inputs: a click on a switch opens or closes it, on a changeover switch throws it to its other contact, and on a logic input changes it between low and high; the picture on the sheet is the state. A push button is closed for as long as the mouse button is held on it. A fuse blows when its current passes its rating, is struck through on the sheet, and a click on it puts a new one in.

The Live Scope: what you click is drawn as it goes, voltage and current, with the least, the most and how often they repeat. Put as many as six scopes side by side (+ on a scope's bar, or View in a New Scope on the right-click menu), each with its own probes. Each scope shows its probes against time, as a spectrum, or as the circuit's frequency response there: gain and phase from 0.1 Hz to 100 MHz, worked out again whenever the circuit changes.

Sound: a speaker is a part with two terminals and its impedance between them, and the voltage across it is played through the computer's sound while the sheet runs, at its true pitch, a stretch of the circuit's time at once (half a second, unless you set another). Sound from the speaker in the panel turns it off. Two of the examples play: a 555 timer's tone and two sine sources beating.

Keys while you sketch: with Keys place parts ticked in the panel, a single key picks up a part while the sheet runs, and each tile shows its key. R is a resistor, C a capacitor, Shift+L an inductor, S a switch, B a push button, U a fuse, D a diode, Z a Zener, L an LED, N and P the transistors, Shift+N and Shift+P the MOSFETs, A an op-amp, H a logic input, E a D flip-flop, J a JK flip-flop, K a counter, V a DC source, F a sine source, Q a square wave, X noise, I a current source, M a voltmeter, Shift+M an ammeter, O a test point, Y a speaker, W a wire, G a ground and T a text. They take the place of the menus those keys open otherwise, for as long as the sheet runs; clear the tick to have the menus back.

Examples to start from: 48 circuits ready drawn (Design › Simulate › Live Simulation Examples, Examples in the panel, or Live Simulation examples on the Home page). Basics, filters, diodes and thyristors, transistors, MOSFETs and relays, op-amps, logic and chips, and sources: from Ohm's law and a voltage divider to a bridge rectifier, a Zener voltage reference, a TRIAC lamp dimmer, a common-emitter amplifier, an astable multivibrator, a relay driver, an integrator, a latch from two gates, a counter on a seven-segment display and a 555 timer flashing an LED or playing a tone. Pick one and it opens as a sheet of its own and runs, with its test points on the scopes and a line on what to try.

Speed is the circuit's time for each second of yours, from a nanosecond to ten seconds, and starts at a pace the eye can follow. Hold stops the circuit where it is, to be read; From the Start begins again at its operating point, or, with Start with everything discharged ticked, with every capacitor empty and no current in any inductor, which is how an oscillator is seen to start. The run ends when its sheet is closed.

Opening a project that was sent as a ZIP archive: File › Open, or a drop on the window, takes the archive as the files in it, so the project opens with its schematics and board. And what the desktop software's newer versions write beside a project for their own use (the project's structure file, previews) no longer opens as a document in front of the project's own when the files are picked together.

PCB: a semi-circular jumper link was drawn between pads of one part that share a Jumper ID, even when the part was not a jumper and copper already joined them. A link, and a jumper's join in the connectivity, now need both: the component's type is Jumper and the pads share a Jumper ID that is not 0, as in the desktop software.
The toolbar's Open is a folder standing open with a document in it, and New is a page with a green plus: the two were easy to take for each other.

The antenna analysis's measured time is given for the processor too: the example board's model of 230,000 cells took 3 seconds on the graphics of an Intel Core Ultra 9 288V and 19 seconds on its processor.

releases.title: Antenna analysis, default primitives you can change, and the fields put in line

items.text: Antenna analysis (Tools › Antenna Analysis, in the PCB editor): an antenna drawn in the board's copper, such as an inverted F, a meander, a patch or a printed dipole, is worked out from the copper itself. Pick the pad it is fed at and its ground, give the frequency, and Konium Designer steps Maxwell's equations through the board and the air round it. It gives the impedance and S11 at your frequency, S11 across the band with the band under −10 dB, the impedance on a Smith chart, and two-part networks that would match the antenna.
items.alt: The example board with the Antenna Analysis panel on the right: fed at the pad FEED against GND, for 2450 MHz from a 50 Ω source. The board is coloured by the current on its copper, red along the inverted F at the top and blue over the ground below it. Beside the cursor on the antenna a read-out gives 53 A/m for 1 W, −5.6 dB of the largest. Under Results: 48.5 + j2.0 Ω and S11 −32.0 dB (VSWR 1.05) at 2450 MHz, the S11 curve with its best match of −51.1 dB at 2435 MHz, under −10 dB from 2227 MHz to 2619 MHz, and the Smith chart.

items.text: How much it radiates and where: the share of the accepted power that is radiated (less the laminate's loss, and the copper's as estimated from the current on it), directivity and gain, the pattern in three cuts, and the pattern as a shape you can turn, with the board's outline inside it.
items.alt: The same board with the panel moved down to the radiation: it radiates 94 % of the power it accepts, the laminate taking 6 %. The pattern is drawn in three cuts, with the figures under it: directivity 3.1 dBi and gain 2.8 dBi. Below them are the pattern as a shape to turn, the ticks for the current on the board and for showing it in motion, and the model's line: 227,994 cells, in 45 s on the processor.

items.text: The current on the copper is laid over the board, red where it is largest, and the cursor reads it. In motion shows the current going through its cycle. Report... saves the figures, the match across the band and the gain round the board as text.

Where the browser has a graphics card it can use (WebGPU), the steps are taken on the card: a model of 230,000 cells, the size of the example board's, took 3 seconds on the graphics of an Intel Core Ultra 9 288V. Without one they are taken on the processor, and a run takes from half a minute to minutes. Both give the same figures. Open the example board from the panel to try it: an inverted F for 2.45 GHz.

What it is: the model is the board's copper as thin sheets, its vias, the laminate with its loss and the air round it. It leaves out the parts on the board, the copper's thickness, solder mask, an enclosure, cables and a hand. Expect the resonance within a few per cent, nearer with finer detail: an estimate to design by, then measure. The User Guide's section says the rest (F1 in the panel).

Long work no longer pauses between its steps on a timer. A browser holds a hidden tab's timers back, so an analysis, the autorouter, automatic placement or an import that was started and left for another tab crawled until the tab was looked at again.

Preferences › Schematic › Default Primitives can be changed: it was a list to read. It lists 31 kinds of schematic object by group; Edit Values opens a kind's own properties (colours, widths, font, text, style), in mils or millimetres, and the next one placed starts from them. Reset and Reset All take them back, Save As and Load move them between browsers, and a changed default is starred. Tab while placing now opens the properties of a wire, a bus and every shape as it is drawn, not only of the objects that follow the cursor: the one being placed takes them and so does the default, unless Permanent is ticked. A font chosen with Tab now reaches the sheet it is placed on.

Preferences › PCB Editor › Defaults: Edit Values works with no board open (it was greyed for seven of its eleven kinds until a board was in front). Both pages are laid out alike: the list with Edit Values and Reset under it, and what the page is for, Save As, Load, Reset All and Permanent beside it.

The analysis panels' fields stand in columns: in Power Analysis, Supply Impedance, Thermal Analysis, EMC Check and Field Solver every box and list starts on one line and is one length, and the EMC Check's rules are in columns too.

More fields put in line in the same pass: a number in Preferences is as long as the lists beside it, with its unit inside its box; the AI page's model list starts where the page's other boxes do; the IPC footprint wizard's single figures line up with its ranges; and the Pad dialog's corner radius no longer stands out of its frame.

The rest of the UI was gone through for the same faults, every command's dialog, every panel and every Preferences page. Preferences' ticks are at their full size, and the kinds under Shift Click To Select keep inside their frame. The small dialogs that ask for one value, such as Jump To Location and Snap Grid, keep their box inside the dialog. Selection Memory's buttons fit their row. In an output job the data sources' lists are one length, and the variant's list is under its name. Sheet Number Spaces in Document Options and Current Variant in Variant Management stay on one line, and the Lock Pins tick in a component's properties is no longer squeezed.

releases.title: Power, thermal and EMC analysis of the board

items.text: Power analysis (Tools › Power Analysis, in the PCB editor): pick a supply net, the part that feeds it and what each load draws. Konium Designer works out the voltage each load is left with, the current in every track, copper area and via of the net and of the net it returns on, and what is over your limits: loads against a voltage drop, tracks and vias against IPC-2221's current for a temperature rise, copper areas against a current density. The copper on the board is coloured by voltage drop or current density, and the cursor reads the place under it.
items.alt: The demo board with the Power Analysis panel on the right: the supply net VIN returning on GND, fed by J1 at 5 V, with U1 drawing 0.8 A. The copper is coloured by voltage drop, the VIN track from blue at J1 to red at U1. Beside the cursor on the track a read-out gives 4.9860 V, 14.00 mV from the source, 37.5 A/mm² and 800 mA in the track. Under Results, U1 is left with 4.9772 V, a drop of 22.8 mV or 0.5 %.

items.text: Thermal analysis (Tools › Thermal Analysis): type what each part dissipates and see the temperature the board settles at, layer by layer: the hottest place, each heated part's board and junction temperature, and the warmest parts, which matters to a capacitor or a crystal beside a regulator. Still air is worked out from how warm each face gets, or you give the coefficients for moving air. The copper's own heat can be added from the power analysis, and Warm-up draws how the board warms over time.
items.alt: The demo board with the Thermal Analysis panel on the right: still air at 25 °C, the board lying flat, U1 given 0.5 W and a junction-to-board resistance of 15 K/W. The board is coloured by temperature, red at U1 through yellow to blue-green at the far end. Beside the cursor a read-out gives 43.9 °C, 18.9 above the air. Under Results, the hottest place is 76.3 °C on the Top Layer, U1's board is at 73.0 °C and its junction at 80.5 °C.

items.text: EMC check (Tools › EMC Check): the layout looked over for the places where a signal's return current has no easy way back: tracks over slots and splits in the copper under them or along its edge, layer changes with no via or capacitor beside them, supply pins of ICs with no capacitor close by, ground copper too far from a via. Nothing is simulated: each rule is geometry, and each finding is a place to click to.

Supply impedance (Tools › Supply Impedance): what a load sees looking into its supply from kilohertz to gigahertz, with the source, every capacitor and the planes' own resonances, against the target that your ripple and current step set. For a switching regulator there is an estimate of the differential-mode noise it conducts back to its input, against the Class A and Class B limits of CISPR 11 and CISPR 32.

Field solver (Tools › Field Solver): a track's impedance from its cross-section, solved rather than taken from a formula: on the surface with its solder mask, under a layer of dielectric, or between two planes; alone or as a pair; with ground copper beside it; with the copper's thickness and etched slope. It takes a layer's figures from the board's stack and finds the width for the impedance you want.

All five work in the browser on the board as it is, offline, and send nothing anywhere. Each has a section in the User Guide's PCB design chapter (F1 in its panel opens it) that says what it counts and what it leaves out: airflow, common-mode noise and the radiated emission of a whole board are not worked out. They are estimates to design by, so measure before relying on a narrow margin.

F1 from a field: pressed while typing in a panel's field, F1 now opens the User Guide at that panel's section (it did nothing there), and a panel you have clicked in counts as the one in use even when the click was on its text. An auto-hide panel tucks away so that the guide can be read.

Place › Interactive Routing with no net: a track started on bare board, or on a pad with no net, now goes on click after click. It stopped after its first segment in every routing mode but Ignore Obstacles, because the segment it had just laid stood in its own way. Copper with no net is no longer in the way of a route with no net, so a board with no netlist can be drawn by hand; copper that belongs to a net still is, and a route with no net is still in a net's way.
A route with no net is pulled to the centre of a pad or a via with no net and ends there, as a net's route does on its own pads.

releases.title: Dragging tracks: boards routed to their clearance, joints, and what a violation is

items.text: Tracks that would not move: with Avoid Obstacles (the default), a track segment could not be dragged at all when the segments joined to it lay at exactly the rule's clearance from another net. They stretch as it moves, and were taken for an obstacle already hit. Tracks are often routed at exactly the clearance, so on such a board many of them stayed where they were. Copper that already lies at its clearance from something, or nearer, now goes anywhere that brings it no nearer; everything else still stops at the clearance.

A piece of a straight run laid in several pieces could not be dragged in any mode: there was no corner for it to slide along. It now steps out of the run through a new 45° segment at each end, cut from the pieces in line with it. A neighbour a fraction of a degree off the line counts as in line.

A selected track's end handle on a joint between segments moved that one end and broke the track in two. The handle is now the joint: every segment that meets there stretches to it, and a via on the joint goes with it. An end on a pad still leaves the pad alone.
The status bar says what stopped a drag: a track, pad or via and its net, a keep-out, the board's edge, or that the tracks either side allow no more.

What a violation marker means: rest the cursor on a marker, or on an object drawn in the marker colour, and the violation is spelled out beside it. That used to need the heads-up display, which is off at first. Right-click › Violations and Shift+V list them as before.

Net names on tracks are dark on a layer given a light colour (they were light on any colour, so unreadable on green or yellow). Use Smart Display Colour now judges a colour as the eye does: a pure green is light, a pure red or blue is not.

A board whose copper regions are kept twice in its file, as the desktop software saves them, opened with a warning in Messages that a primitive record was shorter than expected, preserved and not drawn. Nothing was wrong: a region's second copy had been counted as unread. A record that really cannot be read is now named by its kind.

releases.title: Fixes from a review of the whole program

items.text: The library editors: with the Properties or Requirements panel open, selecting anything in a schematic library or a PCB library stopped Konium Designer with an error screen. Fixed. A panel that fails now says so in its own place and everything else keeps working, so your documents can still be saved.

Files from someone else could run script inside Konium Designer: a requirements document as it was opened (through a picture's file type), a web page or an SVG attached to a requirement when it was opened from there, and a diagram's label when it was edited. All three are closed. A file's type is checked as it is read, an attachment opens in a tab only if a browser merely shows it (a PDF, a picture, plain text) and is saved to the computer otherwise, and the page now refuses any script written into an attribute.

A file cut short no longer hangs Konium Designer. An EAGLE, DipTrace or IPC-2581 file, or a diagram, that ended in the middle of a tag was read again from its start without end, until the browser ran out of memory. A character reference that names no character no longer stops a file from opening.
Large boards: more than about 120,000 tracks, pads or vias added in one step (a Specctra session read back, a hatched pour) failed with "Maximum call stack size exceeded". Fixed.

The Download page: a 26.169 downloaded there did not match its published SHA-256, because the network the site is served through added its analytics script to the file on the way. The site now asks for its pages and the file to be passed on untouched, so check a download against the SHA-256 on the Download page. The installed app and a copy saved from inside Konium Designer (Help › Get Konium Designer on This Computer) were not affected.

releases.title: konium.app is a website, and Konium Designer is at konium.app/app

items.text: konium.app is now Konium Designer's website: what it does and the files it reads and writes, installing it (or downloading it as one file, with its checksum), What's New, answers to common questions (it runs on your computer and works offline), and a form to write to the author. It follows the system's light or dark setting. Konium Designer itself is at konium.app/app.
items.alt: The website's home page: Konium Designer's name and what it is, an Install Konium Designer button and a Download as one file button, and below them the showcase board in the PCB editor.

items.text: An installed Konium Designer moves to its new address by itself, and your settings, recent projects and local history come with it, since the browser keeps them for konium.app. A copy kept on its version (updates or network activity off) stays as it is at the old address until updates are switched on again. A downloaded file is as before; its Update button now opens the website's Download page.

releases.title: Documents in windows of their own; DipTrace and EAGLE both ways; EasyEDA Pro projects; autorouting with Freerouting

items.text: A document in a window of its own: Window › Open In New Window, or a tab dragged out of the window, puts it in a second window run by this one, so the schematic can sit on one monitor and the board on the other. The two share the project, the undo and the clipboard, and a click in one shows the same thing in the other (with Cross Select Mode's Zoom, it zooms there at once). The second window has its own tabs, menus, toolbars and layer tabs; the panels stay in the main window and follow the document last clicked. Drag a tab back, or close the window, and its documents return.
items.alt: Two Konium Designer windows side by side: on the left the demo project's schematic, its 3.3 V regulator circuit, with the regulator U1 picked; on the right, in a window of its own, the demo board, U1 picked there too.

items.text: Shift+drag on a schematic or schematic library puts a copy of what you pressed on under the cursor, as in the desktop software: placed when you let go, in one step to undo, with designators, net labels, ports and pin numbers stepped on as placing again would.

Text in other alphabets: files the desktop software wrote in a Windows code page other than Western (Cyrillic, Greek, Central European, Turkish and others) show their text as written, each file read in the page its words fit best; Preferences › System › General › Text without Unicode chooses one. Changed text goes back in the file's own page, and unchanged files byte for byte. Text in the Symbol font shows as Windows draws it, and sheets in portrait (A1 and the other standard sizes) stand on their end.
items.alt: A schematic sheet written as a Bulgarian system writes it, a row for each script (Latin, Central European, Cyrillic, Greek, Turkish, Hebrew, Arabic, CJK, Vietnamese, symbols) in six faces (Times New Roman, Arial, Arial italic, Courier New, Tahoma, Calibri), and a last row in the Symbol font, the letters W m p a b g D S drawn as Ω μ π α β γ Δ Σ.

items.text: DipTrace both ways: DipTrace's XML export opens as a project (schematics .dchxml, boards .dipxml, component and pattern libraries; a schematic and a board of one name together). On a DipTrace-made board every pad, hole and part lands where DipTrace's own Gerber, drill and placement files put it. File › Export › DipTrace writes the project as DipTrace XML: the schematic, the board and a component library with its patterns. A design read from DipTrace and unchanged goes back as DipTrace wrote it, byte for byte. Read back in, an export keeps every net, part, pad, via, pour and routed length; it has yet to be tried in DipTrace itself.

EAGLE both ways: an EAGLE schematic and board exported for EAGLE unchanged are the files EAGLE wrote, byte for byte. A board changed only by parts moved or turned and nets rerouted is EAGLE's own file with those changes written in, every other element as EAGLE wrote it; changed further, it is written anew with its signals named as EAGLE named them, so the schematic and the board still pair.

EasyEDA Pro projects: File › Export › EasyEDA Pro writes the project as one .epro, the project file EasyEDA Pro imports with File › Import › EasyEDA Professional: a page for each sheet, the board, and the symbols, footprints and devices they use, every net named as the project compiles it, pours with their copper. Read back in, it keeps every part, net, pad, via, pour and routed length, and every pin where it was; it has yet to be tried in EasyEDA Pro itself. Opening EasyEDA Pro projects improves too: the dielectrics in the stack's order, no doubled names beside power flags, and net ports that join only what they touch.

Autorouting with Freerouting: Route › Auto Route › Export Specctra Design... writes the board as a Specctra design (.dsn) for Freerouting or another Specctra autorouter: layers, outline, keep-outs, footprints, parts (bottom ones as Specctra flips them), nets, vias, width and clearance, and the routes already there, locked ones protected. Route it there and save its session (in Freerouting, File › Export as a Specctra Session File); Route › Auto Route › Import Specctra Session..., or opening the .ses with the board in front, puts its routes in place of the board's and pours the pours again round them, in one step to undo. Each pin goes where Freerouting's own code places it; a full round through Freerouting has yet to be tried.

Smaller things: fonts checked across scripts and faces (Latin, Central European, Cyrillic, Greek, Turkish, Hebrew, Arabic, CJK, Vietnamese and symbols; Times New Roman, Arial, Courier New, Tahoma, Calibri), and the interface's own font gains its Central European letters.

releases.title: KiCad, PADS and Cadence both ways; requirements as a tree, a graph and with an adviser

items.text: KiCad both ways: a KiCad project opened in Konium Designer and exported to KiCad again comes back as KiCad had it. What Konium Designer has no place for (KiCad's own pad shapes, curves, text boxes, groups, tuning patterns, fields and settings) is kept with the object it belongs to and written again while that object is unchanged; what you changed goes back as you changed it. On KiCad's own demo projects every board object (495,079) and every schematic object (40,258) comes back the same, setting by setting (two junctions added where KiCad's own rule wants one), with 99.9 % of KiCad's identifiers kept, and so do the libraries' 408 symbols and 326 footprints. The project's settings come back with your changes to rules and net classes merged in; its custom rules and local settings as they were.

PADS both ways: a PADS Layout board or PADS Logic design opened and written back unchanged is the file PADS wrote, byte for byte. A board you changed goes back as PADS wrote it but for what you changed: parts moved, turned or flipped; nets rerouted (a net's stubs and loose stretches as partly routed connections, as PADS keeps them); free texts, drawings, copper, keep-outs and pours changed, added or deleted, each in its own place. It is written in the file's own units and in the line format of its PADS version, PowerPCB 5 to PADS VX. A board changed beyond that is written anew in the file's coordinates and units, with its layer numbers and its decal and part type names. On KiCad's collection of PADS test files (39 boards, 39 designs) every unchanged file comes back byte for byte, and with a part moved, tracks deleted and a text moved, every other part, decal, layer and pour comes back unchanged.

Cadence: an Allegro board (.brd) or an OrCAD Capture design (.dsn) opened and exported for Cadence unchanged is the file Allegro or Capture wrote, byte for byte. Changed, it goes out in the ASCII formats Cadence's own translators read, so Allegro and Capture make their native files themselves. Allegro boards are read as Allegro has them: against Allegro's own extract of two boards, every part's place, turn and side, every net with its pins, every routed track and every via match.

Requirements as a tree: each requirement shows under its parent wherever it is in the document, and giving it a parent moves it there. New Requirement adds one beside the one picked; Move Up and Move Down move it among those at its level, with everything under it. Exports and the compliance report follow the tree. Columns are resized by dragging the edge of their heading; a double-click puts one back.

Connection graph, on the requirements toolbar: the requirements left to right under their parents, coloured by where their verification stands, and on the right the parts, nets, documents and board they are linked to. Click a requirement to light up what it is part of, what it breaks down into and what in the design meets them; click a part or net to show it in the design.
items.alt: The connection graph of a requirements document beside the demo project: Board power broken down into Input range 4.5 V to 5.5 V and 3.3 V rail, the 3.3 V rail into Ripple under 30 mV and Load up to 250 mA (red: failed), the Mechanical and Interfaces sections below, and on the right Net VIN, Part C2, Net +3V3, Part U1, Part J1 and the board; the 3.3 V rail is picked, so it, its parent, its children and the parts and nets they are linked to are lit and the rest faded.

items.text: Requirements Adviser: work through the requirements with an AI model. It reviews them (vague, not verifiable, two in one, repeated or contradicting another), rewrites them, breaks one down, builds the hierarchy, finds what is missing and suggests how each is best verified. Every change comes with its reason, the old wording struck through beside the new; nothing changes until you apply the ones you tick, in one step Undo takes back. It never changes a figure you wrote unless you ask, and leaves [value] where a figure is yours to give.
items.alt: The Requirements Adviser under the requirements table: asked to review them all, it answers that two need work and the 3.3 V rail has no start-up requirement, and proposes a measurable wording for REQ-004 (the old text struck through, the new in green, with its reason) and a new wording and parent for REQ-008, each ticked to apply.

items.text: Mechanical layers: View Configurations sets a mechanical layer's Layer Type (Assembly, Courtyard, 3D Body, Designator and the rest) and its Component Layer Pairs, saved in the board as the desktop software keeps them; a part flipped to the other side takes what it has on a paired layer to that layer's pair. KiCad's fabrication and courtyard layers come in as Assembly and Courtyard layers paired top and bottom, and typed layers go to KiCad's layers of their kind.
The Design Adviser and the Component Builder drop "AI" from their names: it goes without saying.

Smaller things: a layer turned off (in View Configurations, or Ctrl+click on its tab) leaves the tabs along the bottom, so the layers in use are easy to pick; the button beside the menus says Install, and where the browser hasn't offered to install Konium Designer the window says where the browser's own Install is; Help › Get Konium Designer on This Computer works in every copy; KiCad's largest demo board opens in less than half the memory it took.

releases.title: Bug fixes: internal planes and the design rule check

items.text: Internal planes in Gerber, Gerber X2, ODB++ and IPC-2581 output, in the KiCad, EasyEDA and PADS exports and in the plane view now have a clearance round every pad and via of another net and a thermal relief round every one of their own net. Since 26.071 holes were left out of the planes depending on where the board lies in the design space: on most boards, most or all of them, so their vias and through-hole pads were joined to the planes in those outputs. If you made these outputs for a board with internal planes with 26.071 or later, make them again.

Internal planes work when the board is opened in the desktop software: a plane's net is saved as a split plane over the board, the way that software keeps it (it loaded planes saved before with no net), and a board with such a plane gets that software's default Power Plane Connect Style rule if it has none (without it, that software joined nothing through the planes until an edit made it apply its rules). Pads and vias carry their plane connection settings too, as that software writes them. Boards saved by an earlier Konium Designer get all this the next time they are saved.
Thermal reliefs on internal planes cross the air gap at 45 degrees, as the desktop software makes them.

Design rule check: run side by side with the desktop software's own on a 6-layer board of 130 parts with 58 faults put in on purpose, it now finds 1452 of that software's 1569 violations the same way. Silk To Solder Mask and Silk To Silk measure silkscreen text by its strokes; Minimum Solder Mask Sliver reports each sliver once; Acute Angle no longer reports teardrop joins (559 false reports gone); Un-Routed Net counts every piece of copper of a net, tracks joined to no pad too; Un-Connected Pin reports free pads; Board Outline Clearance checks the silkscreen too.

Design rule check, internal planes: pieces of a plane cut off from the rest of it are reported under Un-Routed Net as isolated copper, and thermal reliefs whose conductors reach too little of the plane under the Power Plane Connect Style rule, as the desktop software reports them. On the same board it reports the same 15 pieces of isolated copper as that software, and 8 of its 9 starved thermals (with 3 that it doesn't report). A plane that nothing of its net reaches isn't reported. Net Antennae: a via that passes through an internal plane of its own net is joined to it, so it isn't reported as an antenna.

Rules applied when the board has none of their kind, with the usual defaults, as the desktop software applies them: Net Antennae, Modified Polygon, Routing Layers, and the fabrication and assembly testpoint styles and usage.
The Design Rule Verification Report heads each rule with its values and scopes, such as Clearance Constraint (Gap=10mil) (All),(All), and lists the rules in the desktop software's order.

Smaller things: What's New marks only the newest release as New; the demo board's sample arc and rounded region have no net, so its design rule check is clean; shelving a polygon pour saves the layer and net to restore it to; KiCad export leaves out an empty plane zone where a split plane covers the board, and no longer stops on a zone with a very large number of points.

releases.title: The User Guide and wire links

items.text: Help › User Guide: the whole of Konium Designer explained in a tab of its own, in seven chapters (Getting started, Schematic capture, Libraries and components, PCB design, Outputs and manufacturing, More tools, Reference), with pictures throughout, links between sections and a search across it. F1 opens it at the section for what you are doing: the panel you are working in, else the document in front.
items.alt: The User Guide in a tab beside the demo project's documents, the PCB design chapter's sections listed on the left, open at Wire links: what they are for, the four steps of placing one, and below them a picture of a wire link on the demo board.

items.text: Wire links: Place › Wire Link draws an insulated wire from copper of a net to more copper of the same net on the same side of the board, straight or with bends, where a track can't go. It is a part of its own (W1, W2 and so on) with a pad to solder to at each end. It joins the net, so the connection line goes and the design rule check is satisfied; it is listed in bills of materials with its length, and it shows as a wire in 3D.
items.alt: The demo board in 3D with a wire link in place of the track between U1 and C2: a dark red wire raised above the board, bending in the middle and dropping at each end to a small blob of solder on its pad.

items.text: Preferences › System › Mouse Wheel Configuration: choose what the wheel does on its own and with Ctrl, Shift or Alt: zoom, scroll up and down, scroll sideways, or nothing. The Shortcut Keys sheet shows the wheel as set.

Each key now runs one command in each editor (13 keys were bound to two). Ctrl+N opens File › New; Ctrl+Shift+G on a board sets the snap grid; Ctrl+S and File › Save work in Output Jobs, BOM documents, Draftsman and the other documents too.

Fixed in schematics and libraries: Place › Pin no longer skips a number between runs; Swap ID Pin in a schematic library is kept when it is saved; Show Template Graphics shows and hides a sheet template's graphics (they weren't drawn at all); new sheets take the metric or imperial units chosen in Preferences; Library Component Properties keeps the Standard (No BOM) type.

Fixed on boards and in outputs: the design rule check's Stop when N violations found limits the markers on the board as well; Remove Net Antennas works, with Automatically Remove Loops; an Output Job's Variant Choice sets the variant of every output; the project's Output Path is used; Remove Duplicates applies to IPC-2581, ODB++, pick and place and test point files too; the CAM editor's RFQ report gives the smallest spacing after a clean design check; a multi-board project takes child projects with Add Existing to Project.

Konium Designer is free and runs on donations. Rarely, someone who uses it often sees a small card in the corner asking whether they would like to chip in; it closes with Not now, and I've chipped in stops it for half a year. The starts it counts stay in your browser. Online, its wording is the day's own from konium.app; that request carries nothing about you or your work.

Smaller things: the Offline chip looks the same in every browser; the CAM editor's panel is called CAM; Preferences › Keyboard Shortcuts lists each command once; a few menu letters no longer clash (File › Export Wizard is on W, File › New › 3D Model on O).

releases.title: Scripting and polygon pads

items.text: Scripting: Tools › Scripts, in the PCB and PCB library editors, opens the Scripts panel, where a few lines of JavaScript work on the board or footprint in front: place parts by a rule, renumber designators, add stitching vias, tracks or pads, change nets and widths, or write a report or a file for a manufacturer. A script sees the board in millimetres from its origin, with layers and nets by name, and every change it asks for is made when it ends, as one step Undo takes back.
items.alt: The demo board with the Scripts panel beside it showing the Via fence along selected tracks example; after it ran on the VIN track from J1 to C1, rows of GND vias line both sides of the track, stopping short of C1's pad, and the panel's output says 11 vias on GND, 3 left out as too close to other nets.

items.text: Scripts run in a sandbox, apart from Konium Designer: no network, and no access to your files, other documents or Konium's own storage. A script gets a copy of the board and hands back the changes it wants; it is stopped after 20 seconds, or with Stop. If it fails, the error shows with the line of the script it came from, and nothing is changed.

Six examples to run or start from: parts placed round a circle, designators renumbered by position, a pick-and-place file in JLCPCB's columns, a via fence along selected tracks (clear of other nets), a net report, and pads round a circle in a footprint. Change an example and it becomes your own. A script can make files to save (CSV or text).

Keeping scripts: yours are kept in the browser, and saved and opened as .js files. A project open from its folder keeps its own in a Scripts folder beside the project file, so they go with the project, version control included.

Write with AI: say what a script should do and the AI model chosen in Preferences › System › AI writes it, or changes the one shown. It is sent your request, the script shown when it is to be changed, and the board's layer and net names, designator prefixes, how many objects of each kind it has and how many are selected, never the design itself.

Help › Scripting Reference (F1 in a script): everything a script can use, how it runs, its limits, recipes and JavaScript in brief, in a tab of its own; searchable, with every example ready to copy or to try.
items.alt: The Scripting Reference in a tab beside the demo project's documents, its sections listed on the left, open at Adding objects: a table of the add methods with what each needs and its defaults, an example that puts a GND via at each corner of the board with Copy and Try it, and the start of the Nets section.

items.text: Polygon pads: Tools › Convert › Create Pad from Selected Primitives makes a pad of any shape drawn as one piece from what is selected: tracks and arcs as closed outlines (one inside another a hole, so two circles make a ring), regions and fills as areas. A ring for a microphone, a notched or irregular outline: the copper, its solder mask opening and, on a surface-mount pad, its paste go with the pad, take its net and select as one; the file keeps them as a pad and ordinary regions, which any tool reading the board understands.
items.alt: A microphone footprint in the PCB library editor: a round pad 1 in the middle and, round it, pad 2, a copper ring made from two circles, its solder mask opening shown as a purple edge, inside a circle on the top overlay; the PCB Library panel lists the footprint's two pads, its three regions (copper, solder mask, paste) and the overlay arc.

items.text: Installed, Konium Designer's window can show its own buttons over the page, the title bar folded away: the menu bar now takes the title bar's place, clear of those buttons, and drags the window by its empty parts. The title bar takes the theme's colour.

releases.title: Version control and team projects

items.text: Version control: a project opened from its folder can be put under version control (Project › Version Control › Add Project to Version Control). Every version is kept in a Git repository in the project's folder, which any Git tool can read too, and shared with your team in one of two places: Konium's store, with nothing to set up (a team's key is made in your browser and seals everything before it leaves, so konium.app can't read it; colleagues join with the key, in Preferences › Data Management › Version Control), or your team's own Git server (GitHub, GitLab, Bitbucket, Gitea and others, with your user name and an access token; reached through Konium's relay, which passes it on and keeps nothing, unless you switch the relay off).
items.alt: The demo project under version control: the Projects panel marks each document as unchanged or changed, with a padlock on the schematic Ben Carter is working on and on the board Ana Petrova has locked; over the board, the project's history lists its three versions with when they were made, who made them and what changed, and beside them the file Ben's version changed, the board, with Compare.

items.text: Commit and update: Commit Whole Project lists what changed since the last commit, takes a note of what you did and pushes it to the team. Update Whole Project brings in what the others have pushed; a file changed both in your commits and by someone else is shown with who changed it, to keep yours, theirs, or both (theirs saved beside yours); a file you changed but haven't committed is committed or put back first. Konium Designer looks for the others' changes every few minutes, and the Projects panel marks each document as unchanged, changed, new, out of date or changed on both sides, with arrows on the project for what is waiting to be pushed and to be brought in.

History: the project's history, and each document's (Document History), list the versions with who made each one, when, and the files it changed. Open a version, save it as a file, restore it, or export the whole project as it was as a zip, in Konium's store as on your own server.

Locks: Lock tells the team you are working on a document, and a padlock shows it in the Projects panel (blue yours, amber someone else's) as the others look for changes. A lock doesn't stop anyone: whoever tries to lock it too is told whose it is and since when, and can take it over; changing a document someone else has locked tells you so, once. Your locks go when you commit and push their files (unless you untick that), or with Unlock.

Compare: two versions of a schematic or a board side by side, kept at the same place and zoom, with what was added in green, what was removed in red and what changed in amber, and listed (a part moved, a track widened, a net label renamed). Click a difference to go to it in both. From Document History (Compare with Current), the history's changed files, and the Storage Manager's Local History versions.
items.alt: The demo board as it was in Ana Petrova's version beside the board as it is now: C2 moved nearer the regulator in amber, a new via in green on the right, the track taken out near J1 in red on the left, the rest dimmed; below, the three differences listed with C2 moved 85.4 mil.

items.text: Open Project from Version Control (File menu): a team's project from Konium's store, or a repository on a Git server, into an empty folder, and opened from there. Repository Settings moves a project to another place with all its versions.

Changed: a specification split into requirements runs on Qwen Flash, a cheap text model (always its family's newest), on the Konium service, where it takes one job token, and with an OpenRouter key, whichever model is chosen for drawings; should it fail there, the model chosen does it. A model on your computer or another endpoint still does it itself.
Fixed: pdf.js, which reads datasheets and specifications, updated to a version without a known flaw that let a malicious PDF run script.

releases.title: Requirements

items.text: Requirements: a new document type (.ReqDoc) for a project's requirements. File › New › Requirements makes one; so do the Home page and Add New to Project › Other. Requirements sit under sections, each with an identifier unique across the project (REQ-001 and on; the prefix is yours to set), a title, the requirement in full, its source, type, priority (Must, Should, Could), status (Draft, Approved, Obsolete) and, when it is part of another, its parent. The table lists them with the one picked shown in full beside it (drag the line between them to widen it): add one (Insert), add one under the one picked, add sections, move rows up and down, delete, undo, redo and search.
items.alt: A requirements document in the demo project: requirements under Power, Board and Environment, two of them under the 3.3 V rail requirement, each with its type, priority, status and verification, most of the board's verified by their checks and Low profile failed; on the right the requirement Fits the housing in full, its text with a bold figure, a mounting drawing and a table of hole positions, its source, and an attached PDF of the housing drawing.

items.text: Formatted text, pictures and attached files: a requirement's text is formatted as you type: bold, italic, underline (Ctrl+B, Ctrl+I, Ctrl+U), superscript and subscript, bullet and numbered lists, tables (Tab moves from cell to cell; rows and columns added and deleted where the caret is), links (Ctrl+K), and pictures pasted, dropped or inserted, each shown small, medium, large or full. What is pasted from Word or a web page keeps its formatting as far as these go. Files attached to a requirement (drawings, datasheets, test reports, up to 25 MB each) open in a new tab (PDFs, pictures and text) or are saved. Pictures and files are kept in the .ReqDoc, so it stays one file to save and send; the table marks the requirements that have them with a paperclip.

Verification: each requirement says how it is verified (test, analysis, inspection or review), where that stands (not verified, verified, failed or waived) and a note of the evidence. The foot of the table counts them.

Checks against the design: give a requirement a check and the design is measured for it as you work: the board's copper layers, size and thickness, the tallest part above and below it, parts and BOM lines, the parts' cost per board from the BOM document's prices, the parts' operating temperature (from their parameters), the narrowest track, the smallest hole, the design rule check (run when you ask), compile errors, and whether the project's enclosure fits a space. A check passes, fails, or says why it can't tell yet, and the verification follows it unless you untick that.

The Requirements panel (the Design Compiler button at the bottom right): the project's requirements beside the schematic or the board, searched and filtered (not verified, failed, Must, or linked to the selection), the one picked with its text, pictures and attached files. Link it to the selected parts and nets, or to the sheet or the board itself, and click a link to go back to it in the design, selected and zoomed to. Properties lists the requirements of the selected parts and nets. What you change in the panel goes into the document, one step to undo there.
items.alt: The demo board with the Requirements panel on the right: the project's requirements with how many links each has and where its verification stands, and the regulated 3.3 V rail requirement picked, linked to the part U1 and the net +3V3; U1 selected on the board by following its link.

items.text: Import and export: requirements come in from an Excel workbook or a CSV file, each column matched to a field by its heading (ID, Section, Title, Requirement, and other names such as Req ID, Description, MoSCoW or Compliance; you can change any match), and are shown before they are added; a table (Markdown rows) or a list in a cell comes in formatted. They go out to Excel or CSV, one row each with its text (tables as Markdown rows), verification, its check and what the design measures, its links and the names of its attached files; Import reads such a file back, all but its links, checks, pictures and files.

The compliance report: one page to read, print or send, with the share of requirements verified or waived, counts by state and by priority, what needs attention (failed, and Must requirements not yet verified), and every requirement under its section with its formatted text and pictures and its evidence: its check and what the design measured, the note, its links, its source and the names of its attached files. Open it in a new tab from the toolbar, or save it from Export.

Split a specification with AI: paste a specification, or open it (text, Markdown, Word .docx or PDF), and the AI model chosen in Preferences › System › AI splits it into single requirements in the specification's own words and figures, each with its section, clause, type, priority and how it would be verified. From a Word document, the rows of a table a requirement needs come as a table, and its pictures go with the requirements that refer to them (the model reads where they are, not the pictures themselves). Tick the ones to keep: they are added under their sections, with the specification's name and clause as their source, one step to undo. Only the specification's text and name are sent, nothing of the design.

releases.title: The enclosure designer; ActiveRoute's Route Guide and Pin Swapping

items.text: Enclosure designer: File › New › Enclosure makes a box for your board, made to be 3D printed. It is built round the board as it is (its size, mounting holes and parts) and shown in 3D with the board inside; with no board open, it opens the project's, or asks for the PCB document to build round. The tools down the left put a feature where you click a face of the box, in 3D (a boss, pin, block or rib inside or outside, by the side you click) or in the face view under it. The Features list holds what was found from the board and what you added; the Properties on the right set up the box, or the feature you picked.
